extracted.intended_audience: general public interested in science, law, and public-policy (Planet Money listeners/readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Explaining and evaluating the legal and policy standards that determine whether genetic material (isolated genes, cDNA, modified genes) is patent-eligible, with attention to Supreme Court reasoning and practical effects on testing, research, and industry behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolated natural genes are not patent-eligible (isolation ≠ invention)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Myriad did not create anything. Separating a gene from its surrounding genetic material is not an act of invention," — Supreme Court unanimous ruling invalidating patents on isolated human genes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page reports the Court's holding that merely extracting or isolating a naturally occurring gene does not transform it into a patentable invention. Practical consequence: thousands of gene patents (including Myriad's BRCA claims) were invalidated, freeing researchers and companies to test and study those genes without infringing those patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: cDNA (synthetic DNA) remains patent-eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court made an exception for cDNA, described on the page as "a synthetic version of a gene."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Synthetic constructs (cDNA) created by human manipulation can be treated differently from naturally occurring DNA and may be eligible for patent protection, per the ruling's carve-out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical precedent: 1980 decision allowed patenting of modified living things
rubrics_metrics.description: Until 1980, living things mostly couldn't be patented. But in 1980 the Supreme Court said these new modified genes are inventions, opening the door to patents on genetically modified materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This historical shift underlies the later wave of gene patents: lab-modified organisms and altered genes were treated as patentable inventions, which led patent offices and companies to grant and pursue patents on isolated and modified genetic material through the ensuing decades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability test: invention/creation vs discovery/natural product
rubrics_metrics.description: Central legal/philosophical criterion is whether the claimed subject-matter is a human-made invention (a creation) or merely a discovery of something that exists in nature (a raw material).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page recounts competing metaphors (gold in a mountain, baseball bat carved from a tree, cookie ingredients) used by justices and counsel to probe where the line should be drawn. Assessments should focus on whether the claimed subject involves human ingenuity that meaningfully transforms natural material into something new, not merely isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy balancing: patent incentives versus public access and follow-on innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court and commentators considered whether denying patents on isolated genes would undercut incentives for companies to perform costly gene discovery work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating patent policy or a specific patent claim, weigh incentives for upstream discovery (companies' ability to recoup investment and be motivated to find genes) against harms to downstream research, clinical testing, and public access created by exclusivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents as practical monopolies that can block testing and research
rubrics_metrics.description: Myriad's patents effectively blocked others from offering comprehensive BRCA testing; as a result, a single company was often the only place to get testing, preventing second opinions and independent validation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page documents real-world consequences: restricted availability of tests, higher prices, inability to obtain independent confirmation, and slowed research due to exclusive control over testing and associated data. These impacts are relevant criteria when assessing the social costs of allowing particular patent claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggressive enforcement and data-hoarding exacerbate patent harms
rubrics_metrics.description: Myriad sent letters threatening legal action (and filed a small number of lawsuits) which had the same chilling effect as litigation; it also refused to share its BRCA variant database with the scientific community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate not just the patent right on paper but how the right is enforced and exercised: widespread threats, cease-and-desist letters, and refusal to share clinically relevant data can multiply harms to research, patient care, and scientific progress. Company rationales (e.g., patient privacy) should be weighed against the costs to the research community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinical and ethical concerns from commercialization practices (marketing and incomplete tests)
rubrics_metrics.description: Myriad marketed its test directly to consumers despite a small eligible population; its early test initially failed to screen for several dangerous mutations, potentially giving some customers a false sense of security.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing commercial genetic-testing operations tied to patents, consider ethical criteria such as appropriate targeting of marketing, completeness and accuracy of tests, transparency about limitations, cost burdens on patients, and availability of follow-up or improved testing without excessive additional cost.
